result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.bfs_beam_edges()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: >- Get the edges of a breadth-first search that follows only the most promising neighbors. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.bfs_beam_edges()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: >- Get the edges of a breadth-first search that follows only the most promising neighbors. title: >- [Graph.bfs_beam_edges()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: >- Get the edges of a breadth-first search that follows only the most promising neighbors. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get the edges of a breadth-first search that follows only the most promising neighbors. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L54988-L55107){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.bfs_beam_edges( source, value, width=None, mode="out", ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![BFS beam edges](../assets/graphs/bfs-beam-edges.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A six-node tree searched from A (outlined) with a beam of width 1; every node carries its score in a badge. A's best neighbor is C (5), not B (1), and C's best is F (3), not E (2), so the search follows the accent edges A-C and C-F only. B, and with it the top-scoring D (9), is never reached. The card lists (A, C) and (C, F)." width="100%"} Beam search is a breadth-first search on a budget: at each node it ranks the neighbors by `value=` and follows only the best `width=` of them, so the search fans out along high-scoring nodes and skips the rest. It is a cheap way to explore a huge graph (or one built on demand) when a score says which way looks promising, for example following the most-cited papers outward from a starting paper, or the best-rated items in a recommendation graph. Nodes outside the beam are only skipped from that node: another node can still reach them. As in a plain BFS, each node is reached once, so the result is a tree. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The starting node, as an integer ID or a string label. [value]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[Callable[[int], float], str, dict]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The score that ranks neighbors (higher is better): a function taking a node ID and returning a number, the name of a numeric node attribute, or a `{node: number}` dictionary. Every node that gets ranked needs a score, including neighbors that were already visited (the source among them). [width]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : How many of each node's neighbors to follow. If `None` (default), all of them, which makes this an ordinary BFS that visits neighbors best first. [mode]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["out"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Which way to follow edges on a directed graph: `"out"` (default), `"in"`, or `"all"`. Ignored for undirected graphs. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[tuple[int, int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `(parent, child)` node-ID pairs in the order the children were discovered. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the node does not exist, `width=` is not a positive integer, `mode=` is invalid, or a ranked neighbor has no numeric score (or a NaN one). [TypeError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `value=` is not a function, an attribute name or a dictionary. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~bfs_edges`) : The edges of a full breadth-first search. ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Each node's distinct neighbors are sorted by score, highest first, with ties kept in edge insertion order, and the first `width` of them are followed if not yet visited. Visited neighbors still take up places in the beam, as in NetworkX. Each node is scored once, when it is first ranked. Matches NetworkX's `bfs_beam_edges`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} From A, with a beam of width 1, the search follows only each node's highest-scoring neighbor: ::: {#c5e45575 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(list("ABCDEF")) g.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "E"), ("C", "F")]) g.set_node_attrs("score", {"A": 0, "B": 1, "C": 5, "D": 9, "E": 2, "F": 3}) label = g.get_label_from_id [(label(p), label(c)) for p, c in g.bfs_beam_edges("A", value="score", width=1)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [('A', 'C'), ('C', 'F')] ``` ::: ::: B is never reached, so neither is its high-scoring neighbor D. A wider beam takes both of A's neighbors: ::: {#34e80b8b .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} [(label(p), label(c)) for p, c in g.bfs_beam_edges("A", value="score", width=2)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [('A', 'C'), ('A', 'B'), ('C', 'F'), ('C', 'E'), ('B', 'D')] ``` ::: :::
